# Experiments

This chapter describes your experimental set up and evaluation. It should also
produce and describe the results of your study. The section titles below offer
a typical structure used for this chapter.

<!--
WRITING GUIDE for Chapter Four

HTML comments are stripped from the PDF and the website; they are here for you
to read while you draft.

WHAT A READER NEEDS FROM THIS CHAPTER

1. Which research question each experiment answers.
2. Exactly what was run, so that the experiment could be repeated.
3. What counted as success, decided before you ran anything.
4. The data itself, in a table or figure, not only in prose.
5. What the data supports, separated from what you hope it supports.

Never introduce an experiment in this chapter that Chapter Three did not
describe, and never report a metric that Chapter Three did not define.

A NEGATIVE RESULT IS STILL A RESULT

If the artifact did not beat the baseline, say so, and then do the most valuable
work in the chapter: explain why. Was the dataset too small? Was the comparison
unfair? Did the implementation not exercise the idea? An honest negative finding
with a careful explanation earns more credit than a positive finding you cannot
defend. Do not quietly omit runs that went badly.
-->

## Research Questions and Experiment Mapping

<!--
List your research questions and the experiment that addresses each one:

| Research question | Experiment | Metric | Success threshold |
|:------------------|:-----------|:-------|:------------------|
| RQ1: ...          | ...        | ...    | ...               |

Two or three focused questions are better than six that overlap. Each row must
have a non-empty entry in every column; a blank threshold means you will not be
able to say whether the experiment succeeded.
-->

## Experimental Design

Especially as it pertains to responsible computing, if conducting experiments or
evaluations that involve particular ethical considerations, detail those issues here.

<!--
Restate the design from Chapter Three in enough operational detail to repeat it:
the machine, the inputs, the number of repetitions, the order of conditions, and
how you controlled for differences that are not part of the study. State what
you would have done if a run crashed or produced no output, and then say whether
that happened.
-->

## Baseline and Success Criteria

<!--
A result means nothing without a comparison. Name the baseline: the existing tool,
the unmodified version of your system, the human process, or a naive method.
Explain why that baseline is the fair comparison. Then state the threshold for
success in numbers, and say whether the threshold came from the literature, from
a practical requirement, or from your own judgement.
-->

## Evaluation

<!--
For each metric, say how it is computed and in what units, then report the value
with some indication of variation: repeated runs, a confidence interval, a
standard deviation, or a clear statement that the measurement is deterministic.
Where you use statistics, name the test and check its assumptions; a p-value
without a stated test is not evidence.

Every table and figure needs three things: a caption that explains what is
shown, a sentence in the text that refers to it, and a sentence that interprets
it. "Table 2 shows the runtimes" is a reference; "Table 2 shows that the
optimized version is faster only when the input exceeds 10,000 records, which
suggests that setup cost dominates on small inputs" is an interpretation.
-->

## Results

<!--
Present the outcomes in the order of your research questions. For each one:
restate the question in a sentence, point to the evidence, state the finding,
and state how confident you are. Keep observation and interpretation in separate
sentences so that a reader can tell which is which.
-->

## Unexpected and Negative Findings

<!--
Report results that did not fit your expectations, including runs that failed.
Explain what you think caused each one and what it implies for the method or for
future work. This section strengthens a thesis; it does not weaken it.
-->

## Threats to Validity

<!--
Organize the discussion with the standard categories, keeping only those that
apply to your study:

- **Internal validity** — could something other than your treatment explain the
  result (ordering effects, caching, machine load, a bug in the harness)?
- **External validity** — how far do the results generalize beyond the datasets,
  languages, platforms, or users you studied?
- **Construct validity** — do your metrics actually measure the concept you
  claim to measure (does line coverage really mean test quality)?
- **Conclusion validity** — are the statistical or logical inferences sound
  given the number of runs and the variance you observed?

For each threat, say what you did to mitigate it. A threat you cannot mitigate
should be named anyway, because your readers will find it.
-->
